newsitem.title: BELGIUM: U.S. considers new ways to freeze out Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: U.S. considers new ways to freeze out Milosevic.

text.p: The United States is considering new ways to pressure Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic into acknowledging opposition success at local elections, including banning new trade and official contacts with Belgrade.

U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Europe John Kornblum told reporters that the major powers' Contact Group on former Yugoslavia had ruled out international sanctions against Serbia, but individual countries were independently examining ways of freezing out Milosevic.

"The general consensus is that we are not at the point to pursue (unified) sanctions," Kornblum said after a meeting of the group -- made up of senior officials from the United States, Britain, Germany, France, Italy and Russia -- in Brussels.
But Kornblum said Washington was looking into a four-point "action plan" by which the U.S. could unilaterally help democratisation in Serbia.

The plan was to freeze trade and official relations with Serbia; ensure continued international focus by international organisations on the situation; increase democratisation assistance, and; target structural obstacles to democracy.
The Contact Group was meeting to discuss ways of putting pressure on Belgrade to accept a report by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
The report, compiled by former Spanish Prime Minister Felipe Gonzalez, says the Serbian opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition won 14 of 18 cities, including Belgrade, in recent municipal elections.

Kornblum said the Contact Group believed "concerted diplomatic pressure" should continue to be applied to Milosevic "so that he is made fully aware of the dangerous consequences for his country and the region should the current situation continue".
Kornblum admitted, however, that this was proving difficult as the Serbian leader appeared to have isolated himself from any contact with the international community over the affair.
"He is taking his country down the road to ruin," said Kornblum. "The country is going down a bad path."
In Belgrade, Serbian opposition leaders promised deafening, round-the-clock traffic jams in the city centre on Saturday, the 55th straight day of peaceful protests against the poll fraud.
A senior political source told Reuters, however, that Milosevic was likely soon to endorse the OSCE report and call for forming a coalition government. Kornblum said he was unaware of the move.
Expanding on the four-point plan, a statement from U.S. officials said Washington was considering denying an application by Yugoslav Airlines (JAT) for landing rights in the U.S.
The U.S. would also swiftly approve an assistance programme that would focus on helping independent media and electoral organisations in a country where news is tightly controlled by the government.

Washington also wanted to discourage trade missions and high-level visitors to Belgrade and maintain an "outer wall" of sanctions including prohibiting financial institutions from contact with Serbia.

Investigations into reports of financial crimes and criminal activity by state-owned enterprises and trading groups which threaten "civil society and market economy" could also be encouraged, it said.
Despite Washington's apparent lone concrete action, Kornblum stressed that the Contact Group was united in backing diplomatic action rather than sanctions at international level.
"The feeling is that we should continue with diplomatic pressure at this time," Kornblum said. "Sanctions will not resolve the present crisis in Yugoslavia."
Russia's representative on the Contact Group, Alexander Arsenenor, said there had to be a "persistent search for honest dialogue" rather than sanctions.
"This (election dispute) is an internal matter for Yugoslavia but everyone is aware it has wider implications," he said.

Britain's Emyr Jones-Parry told reporters he fully endorsed the Contact Group's approach. "If they (the Serbian leadership) take the right path there is a possibility of success," he said. "If they don't, they must face the consequences."
